stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. I'd like an ice cream. Are you having \(\underline{\text{one}}\) too?
optB: Pronoun
solution:
The underlined word stands in place of the noun phrase an ice cream, already named in the previous sentence, instead of naming or describing anything itself.
A word used in place of a noun is a pronoun.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. My parents lent me the money. \(\underline{\text{Otherwise}}\), I could not have afforded the trip.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word links the idea of its sentence back to the one before, but it does so from inside a separate sentence, after a full stop.
A conjunction cannot do that; it must stand between the two clauses it joins.
The word is also free to move within its own clause, as in I could not otherwise have afforded the trip, which no conjunction can do.
That mobility, together with the sentence boundary, makes it a linking or conjunctive adverb.
Matches option B.
reviewNote: Disputed, and worth a teacher's decision before the key is issued. The matching bank question prints the same four choices in the same order and keys Conjunction, as several Indian answer keys do, because the word means 'or else'. Answered Adverb on two grounds. (i) Grammar: the word heads a separate sentence after a full stop and is freely movable inside its own clause ('I could not otherwise have afforded the trip'); a conjunction can do neither, and the standard reference grammars class this word as an adverb. (ii) Internal consistency: question 18 of this same paper puts 'Besides' in exactly the same frame, with Conjunction printed as a choice, and the answer there is Adverb; keying Conjunction here would make the paper contradict itself.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She wrote me an \(\underline{\text{anguished}}\) letter from her prison cell.
optB: Verb
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun letter and tells what kind of letter it was.
A word that qualifies a noun in this way is an adjective; here it is a past participle used adjectivally.
Matches option C.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. There is \(\underline{\text{a}}\) visitor for you.
optB: Definite Article
solution:
The underlined word is an article.
It does not point to any particular known visitor, only to one visitor of an unspecified kind, so it is the indefinite article; the definite article is the word the.
Matches option C.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She came \(\underline{\text{slowly}}\) up to the main door.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word tells how she came, so it modifies the verb came.
A word that modifies a verb is an adverb; this one is formed from the adjective slow by adding -ly.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{They}}\) are all going to attend the function.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word is the subject of the sentence and stands in place of a plural noun already known from the context.
A word used instead of a noun is a pronoun; this one is a personal pronoun.
Matches option C.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. His \(\underline{\text{happiness}}\) was obvious, as he had won unprecedented appreciation for his hard work.
optB: Abstract noun
solution:
The underlined word names a feeling, not a person, place or thing that can be seen or touched.
A noun naming a quality, state or feeling is an abstract noun; this one is formed from the adjective happy.
A collective noun would name a group, and a common noun a class of concrete things, so neither label fits.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. I \(\underline{\text{wonder}}\) if at times it rains to give us some respite from the dull moments of life.
optB: Conjunction
solution:
The underlined word follows the subject I and states what the speaker does, taking the whole clause beginning if at times as its object.
A word expressing an action or a state in this way is a verb.
The same word is a noun in a phrase such as the wonders of nature, but that is not its use here.
Matches option C.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{righteous}}\) always emerge victorious.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word is normally an adjective, but here it follows the and has no noun after it, and it takes the plural verb emerge.
The pattern the plus adjective denotes the whole class of such people and is plural in sense and in agreement.
In this sentence, therefore, the word functions as a plural noun.
Matches option A.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Alas}}\)! He has been defeated.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word stands alone before an exclamation mark and expresses sudden grief; it neither joins nor modifies anything in the sentence.
A word used as an isolated exclamation of feeling is an interjection.
Matches option C.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He has been living in the jungle for long \(\underline{\text{and}}\) he knows all the animals here.
optB: Coordinating conjunction
solution:
The underlined word joins two clauses, He has been living in the jungle for long and he knows all the animals here, each of which could stand alone as a sentence.
A conjunction joining two grammatically equal units is a coordinating conjunction; a subordinating one would have made the second clause dependent on the first.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Where}}\) there is peace for some time, there will be prosperity.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word introduces the clause there is peace for some time and relates it to the main clause as a statement of place; it asks nothing, so it is not interrogative here.
It does not stand in place of a noun, so it is not a pronoun, and it does not qualify a noun, so it is not an adjective.
It is a relative adverb of place, that is, an adverb.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. A \(\underline{\text{zero}}\) is a zero always.
optB: Compound noun
solution:
The underlined word follows the article A and is the subject of the verb is, so it names a thing.
A word that names something and can take an article is a noun, and this one is a single word, so it is not a compound.
Matches option A.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. May you be blessed with \(\underline{\text{all}}\) good things of life.
optB: Adverb
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] No printed option is correct. The underlined word qualifies the following noun phrase, so it is a determiner or adjective of quantity, and neither class is offered.

The underlined word stands before the noun phrase good things of life and tells how many of them are meant, so in this sentence it qualifies a noun.
A word of quantity used before a noun in this way is a determiner, or in the older terminology an adjective of quantity, and neither of those is printed here.
It is certainly not a verb, not an adverb and not a noun, so of the four printed choices the nearest is the class to which this word is standardly assigned, the one it belongs to when it stands on its own, as in All is well.
Matches option D.
reviewNote: Defective. In this sentence the underlined word qualifies the noun phrase 'good things of life', so its class here is determiner, or adjective of quantity in traditional terms; neither is among the printed choices, so no printed choice is strictly correct. The remaining three are impossible in this sentence, so the pronoun choice has been keyed as the closest, this word being standardly classed as an indefinite pronoun or determiner. Anyone marking this question should treat it as unreliable rather than penalise a blank.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The lake is one of the more \(\underline{\text{beautiful}}\) ones in the country.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun ones and tells what kind, so it qualifies a noun.
The word more before it is the comparative marker belonging to it, which confirms that the underlined word is the one being compared, and only adjectives and adverbs are compared in this way.
Matches option A.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Honesty}}\) is the best policy.
optB: Pronoun
solution:
The underlined word names a quality, not an object that can be counted: it has no plural and takes no article here, and one cannot speak of two honesties.
A noun that cannot be counted or pluralised is an uncountable noun, and the printing of the countable and the uncountable choices side by side shows that countability is the contrast being tested.
A common noun names a class of concrete things such as boy or city, which does not fit a word naming an abstract quality.
Matches option D.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The conclusions that they came to was highly \(\underline{\text{questionable}}\).
optB: Adjective
solution:
The underlined word stands after the linking verb and describes the subject, the conclusions.
A word that describes or qualifies a noun, whether standing before it or after a linking verb, is an adjective.
The printed verb was should be were, but that slip in agreement does not affect the class of the underlined word.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. I don't think I'll come out on Saturday. I have a lot of work to do. \(\underline{\text{Besides}}\), I don't really like parties.
optB: Adverb
solution:
The underlined word heads a separate sentence, after a full stop, and adds a further reason to what has just been said.
A conjunction must stand between the two clauses it joins, and a preposition must be followed by an object, as in besides the work; neither applies here.
A linking word used freely at the head of a sentence in this way is a conjunctive adverb.
Matches option B.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{bottomline}}\) is that we have to make a decision today.
optB: Pronoun
solution:
The underlined word follows the article The and is the subject of the verb is, naming the essential point of the matter.
A word that names something and can take an article is a noun.
Matches option A.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{most}}\) beautiful actor of the industry was awarded today.
optB: Numeral
solution:
The underlined word stands before the adjective beautiful and forms its superlative degree, so what it modifies is an adjective, not a noun.
A word that modifies an adjective is an adverb; the noun actor is qualified by beautiful, not by the underlined word.
Matches option C.

optA: A difficult situation involving several hidden problems
optB: An imaginary or illusory discovery
optC: A person who is difficult to understand
optD: A successful discovery made after careful investigation
solution:
A mare builds no nest, so a mare's nest is a discovery that looks important but turns out to be imaginary or worthless.
A successful discovery made after careful investigation is its exact opposite, and a situation full of hidden problems is a hornet's nest.
Matches option B.

optB: A controversial issue that causes public disagreement
optC: A difficult problem requiring great courage
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] Defective twice over. No printed option gives the meaning of the idiom, which is an anticlimax or a disappointing failure; and two of the four options carry identical text. The question cannot be graded fairly and should be dropped from scoring.

A damp squib is a firework too damp to go off, so the idiom means an anticlimax, something expected to be impressive that turns out to be a disappointing failure.
No printed choice carries that meaning.
Of the four printed, the nearest is the one that at least describes an event turning out badly; a public controversy and a task demanding courage share nothing with the idiom.
Matches option A.

optB: To openly oppose a powerful person
optC: To have a private or selfish interest in a matter
optD: To make every effort to achieve a difficult goal
solution:
To have an axe to grind is to have a private or selfish interest behind what one says or does.
The idiom is about concealed self-interest, not about revenge, open defiance or strenuous effort.
Matches option C.

optA: An endless process or series of delays
optB: A secret plan designed to deceive others
optC: A complicated task that can eventually be completed
optD: A sudden change in someone's opinion
solution:
In the Odyssey, Penelope wove a shroud by day and unpicked it by night to put off her suitors, so a Penelope's web is work deliberately spun out and never finished.
The whole point of the allusion is that it can never be completed, which rules out the choice calling the task eventually completable.
Matches option A.

optA: A person admired for exceptional courage
optB: A traditional practice followed by everyone
optC: A person protected from physical danger
optD: A person or thing regarded as beyond criticism
solution:
A sacred cow is a person, institution or custom so revered that it is treated as being beyond criticism or change.
The idiom is about immunity from criticism, not about courage, about physical protection, or about a merely widespread custom.
Matches option D.

optB: Extremely observant and watchful
optD: Unable to understand a complicated matter
solution:
Argus, in Greek myth, was a watchman with a hundred eyes, so Argus-eyed means extremely observant and watchful, letting nothing pass unnoticed.
It describes keenness of observation, not groundless suspicion or speed of decision.
Matches option B.

optB: Exaggerated praise that is not sincere
optC: An insulting remark disguised as praise
solution:
A left-handed compliment is a remark framed as praise but carrying a slight or an insult inside it, as in You look almost intelligent today.
Matches option C.

optA: A troublesome situation that causes further trouble when disturbed
optB: A place where many people gather together
optC: A dangerous person hiding among harmless people
optD: A difficult task requiring great courage
solution:
A hornet's nest is a situation full of trouble which, once disturbed, releases a swarm of further trouble; hence the expression to stir up a hornet's nest.
Matches option A.

optA: A complicated plan requiring several stages
optB: A secret agreement between powerful people
optC: A temporary solution to a permanent problem
optD: An insecure plan or arrangement likely to collapse
solution:
A house of cards is a plan or arrangement so unsound that the slightest disturbance brings the whole of it down.
Matches option D.

stem: A red rag to a bull
optA: Something that reveals a person's weakness
optB: Something certain to provoke or anger someone
optD: Something that unexpectedly brings people together
solution:
A bull is said to charge at the sight of red, so a red rag to a bull is anything certain to provoke or enrage a particular person.
Matches option B.

optA: Being uncertain about what decision to make
optB: Competing peacefully for the same objective
optC: Being openly hostile towards each other
solution:
At daggers drawn describes two parties so bitterly hostile to each other that they are on the point of open fighting.
Hostility is essential to the idiom, which rules out both peaceful competition and calm discussion.
Matches option C.

optA: Being completely perplexed and not knowing what to do
optB: Being physically exhausted after hard work
optC: Being unwilling to accept an unpleasant truth
optD: Being unable to remember an important fact
solution:
To be at one's wit's end is to have exhausted every idea and be completely perplexed about what to do next.
The exhaustion is mental, not physical, so the choice about being tired after hard work does not fit.
Matches option A.

optB: In opposition to or inconsistent with
optD: In competition for the same position
solution:
To be at variance with something is to differ from it, to be in opposition to it or inconsistent with it, as when a statement is at variance with the facts.
Matches option B.

optA: In a state of strong disagreement
optB: In a situation involving two difficult choices
optC: In a state of financial difficulty
optD: In a state of disorder or confusion
solution:
At sixes and sevens means in a state of complete disorder and confusion, with nothing properly arranged.
The choice naming strong disagreement describes being at loggerheads rather than this idiom.
Matches option D.

optA: At the beginning of an important event
optB: Immediately after a crisis has ended
solution:
The eleventh hour is the last hour before midnight, so at the eleventh hour means at the very last moment, only just before it is too late.
Matches option C.

optA: To devise a new plan after an unsuccessful idea
optB: To abandon a project permanently
optC: To begin carrying out an approved plan
optD: To return to a place after completing a successful plan
solution:
When a design fails, the engineer goes back to the drawing board, that is, starts planning afresh from the beginning.
The idiom implies a fresh attempt, so abandoning the project permanently is its opposite.
Matches option A.

optB: Following the wrong approach or looking in the wrong place
optC: Attempting a task impossible for everyone
optD: Refusing to accept a clearly correct solution
solution:
A dog baying at the foot of the wrong tree is pursuing its quarry in the wrong place, so the idiom means to follow a mistaken line of enquiry or to look in the wrong place.
It carries no suggestion of a deliberate false accusation.
Matches option B.

optA: Choosing between two equally attractive opportunities
optB: Facing a choice between success and failure
optC: Moving from a difficult situation to an easier one
solution:
Scylla and Charybdis were a monster and a whirlpool set on opposite sides of a narrow strait, so a sailor who avoided one ran into the other.
To be between them is therefore to be caught between two equally unpleasant alternatives.
Matches option D.

optB: Tolerate someone's behaviour patiently
optC: Suffer the greatest impact of something
solution:
The brunt is the main force or shock of an attack, so to bear the brunt of something is to take the heaviest part of its impact.
Matches option C.

optA: Avoid addressing the main topic directly
optB: Postpone a decision until the final moment
optD: Refuse to accept responsibility for a mistake
solution:
The image is of beating the bushes around the quarry instead of driving it out; the idiom means to approach a subject indirectly and avoid coming to the point.
Matches option A.

optA: Warn people about an approaching danger
optB: Expose a secretly dishonest person
optD: Undertake a difficult or seemingly impossible task
solution:
In the fable the mice agree that a bell round the cat's neck would save them, but not one of them dares to fasten it; to bell the cat is therefore to take on a dangerous or seemingly impossible task for the common good.
Merely warning people of an approaching danger is what the bell would achieve, not what the idiom names.
Matches option D.

optA: Change one's opinion because of pressure
optB: Make every possible effort to help or accommodate someone
optC: Give up one's principles to avoid conflict
optD: Accept defeat after an unsuccessful attempt
solution:
To bend over backwards is to go to extreme lengths, well beyond what could reasonably be expected, in order to help or accommodate someone.
Matches option B.

optB: Slightly different from the expected answer
optC: Irrelevant to the matter under discussion
solution:
The mark is the target; something beside the mark misses it altogether and therefore has no bearing on the matter in hand.
The idiom means irrelevant, not merely slightly inaccurate.
Matches option C.

optA: An enemy who openly challenges you
optB: A person who frequently changes sides
optC: A person who secretly takes advantage of an opportunity
optD: A deceitful or treacherous person who hides hostile intentions
solution:
A snake in the grass is a person who seems harmless but is secretly treacherous and means one harm.
The concealment is essential, so an enemy who challenges one openly is not the sense.
Matches option D.

optA: An imaginary world created through ambition
optB: A state of happiness based on ignorance of potential trouble
optC: A place where foolish people are easily controlled
optD: A temporary escape from an unpleasant situation
solution:
To live in a fool's paradise is to be happy only because one is ignorant of the trouble that is coming; the contentment rests on a false view of things.
Matches option B.

optA: A sudden physical or emotional surprise
optB: A punishment for committing a serious offence
optC: A severe setback or instance of unfair treatment
solution:
A kick in the teeth is a sudden and severe setback, or a piece of grossly unfair treatment, especially from someone whose support was expected.
Matches option C.

optA: A compromise reached after a serious dispute
optB: The most profitable choice among several options
optC: A universally accepted rule of behaviour
optD: A moderate course between two extremes
solution:
The golden mean, an idea from Aristotle's ethics, is the desirable middle course lying between two extremes.
It is a principle of moderation, not a compromise negotiated after a quarrel.
Matches option D.

optA: Officially approved by a government authority
optB: Honest, open and without any secret dealings
optC: Conducted publicly in front of everyone
optD: Free from every possibility of disagreement
solution:
Cards played above the board, in full view and not beneath it, cannot be tampered with; so above board means honest and open, with nothing concealed.
Matches option B.

stem: A chip of the old block
optA: A child who inherits property from a parent
optB: A person who follows the same profession as a parent
optC: A person who resembles a parent in character or qualities
optD: A person who inherits only a parent's weaknesses
solution:
A chip cut from a block is of the same material as the block, so the idiom describes a child who resembles a parent in character or qualities.
It is about likeness of character, not about inheriting property or following the same profession.
Matches option C.

optB: A warning about a danger already known
optC: A planned change producing surprising results
optD: A sudden and unexpected event, especially an unpleasant one
solution:
A bolt of lightning out of a clear blue sky arrives with no warning at all, so the idiom means a sudden and wholly unexpected event, usually an unwelcome one.
Matches option D.
